entries.title: Road Signs
entries.text: Road Signs. Road signs communicate rules, hazards, and directions through consistent shapes and colors. This lesson teaches you how to recognize regulatory, warning, guide, and work-zone signs quickly so you can react before a hazard reaches you.

entries.title: Shapes and Colors
entries.text: Shapes and Colors. Road signs in Florida follow national standards, so their shape and color tell you the general message before you read a single word. An octagon is always a STOP sign, and a downward-pointing triangle is always YIELD. A vertical rectangle is usually regulatory, while a horizontal rectangle is often a guide sign. A diamond warns you that a hazard is ahead, and a pennant shape marks the start of a no-passing zone. Color carries meaning just as strongly as shape. Red means stop or prohibition, and yellow warns of a condition to prepare for. White with black text is regulatory, meaning the rule is enforceable. Green guides you to destinations, blue points to services such as gas, food, and lodging, and orange marks construction or maintenance. Brown highlights recreational and cultural places. Learning these patterns lets you read a sign at a glance, even when the text is small or partly blocked by a truck. That split second matters when you are choosing a lane or slowing for something you cannot yet see.

entries.title: Regulatory Signs
entries.text: Regulatory Signs. Regulatory signs tell you what you must or must not do, and disobeying them is a traffic violation. Common examples include speed limit signs, stop and yield signs, do not enter, one way, and no turn on red. Most are white with black or red markings, and they are placed where the rule actually takes effect rather than far in advance. A speed limit sign shows the maximum legal speed under good conditions. It is a ceiling, not a target to reach, so you may drive slower whenever weather, traffic, or the road surface makes the posted speed unsafe. Signs such as no parking or no left turn apply exactly where they are posted and may include specific times or days. When a regulatory sign and a warning sign appear together, the regulatory sign controls the rule while the warning sign simply tells you what is coming. Reading the entire sign, including arrows and small text, prevents confusion at intersections where several rules meet.

entries.title: Warning Signs
entries.text: Warning Signs. Warning signs are usually yellow diamonds with black symbols, and they alert you to a change in road conditions ahead. They do not create a rule on their own; they tell you to slow down, look, and prepare to adjust. Examples include curve ahead, intersection ahead, pedestrian crossing, slippery when wet, and animal crossing. Some warning signs add a small rectangular plaque underneath, such as a suggested speed for a curve or the distance to the condition. A yellow diamond with a traffic signal symbol warns that a signal is ahead and may be hard to see. A diamond with two opposing arrows shows the direction in which the road curves. Because warning signs describe hazards you cannot see yet, the right response is to ease off the accelerator and scan the road ahead. Rushing past a warning sign at full speed leaves you no time to react if the hazard turns out to be exactly as described.

entries.title: Guide and Service Signs
entries.text: Guide and Service Signs. Guide signs direct you to destinations, routes, and services, and they are informational rather than regulatory. Green signs with white text show exits, distances, and highway names. Blue signs point to services such as gas, food, lodging, and hospitals. Brown signs mark parks, historic sites, and recreation areas. On interstates, guide signs tell you which lane you need well before an exit so you can change lanes calmly. Mile markers help you describe your location if you call for help. Route markers identify numbered highways, including U.S. routes and Florida state routes. Guide signs are easy to read if you look for them early, but you should never stop or swerve suddenly to catch one. If you miss an exit, continue to the next one rather than backing up or crossing a median, which is illegal and dangerous.

entries.title: Work-Zone Signs
entries.text: Work-Zone Signs. Orange signs and channeling devices mark construction and maintenance zones, and they often include temporary speed limits. Orange warns of workers, equipment, and changing pavement. Fines for speeding in a work zone can be higher than usual, and a flagger symbol means a person may be controlling traffic with a paddle. Work zones can change from one day to the next, so the lane you drove yesterday may be closed today. Reduce speed as soon as you see the first orange sign, increase the space ahead of you, and follow the directions of flaggers and pavement markings even when they differ from the usual pattern. Rear-end crashes are common in work zones because traffic slows unexpectedly. Watching the vehicles several cars ahead, not just the one directly in front of you, gives you more warning when traffic bunches up.

entries.title: Reading Signs at Speed
entries.text: Reading Signs at Speed. Good drivers read signs early and process them without staring. Keep your eyes moving so you catch a sign while it is still readable, then glance back to the road. Using shape and color first, and the words second, lets you understand the message in an instant. Signs are placed where drivers can see and react, so if a sign surprises you, you may be driving too fast for the conditions or not scanning far enough ahead. Large overhead signs on highways are designed to be read from a distance, but you still need to choose your lane early. If glare, rain, or darkness reduces visibility, slow down and increase your following distance so you can still read signs in time. Clean headlights and a clear windshield also make signs easier to see at night.

entries.title: Traffic Signals & Road Markings
entries.text: Traffic Signals & Road Markings. Traffic signals and pavement markings tell you when to stop, when to go, and where your lane is. This lesson explains steady and flashing signals, turn arrows, and the meaning of white and yellow road lines so you can read the road surface itself.

entries.title: Steady Signals
entries.text: Steady Signals. A steady red light means stop completely at the stop line, before the crosswalk, or before the intersection when there is no line. Once stopped, you may generally turn right unless a sign prohibits it, and you may turn left from a one-way street onto another one-way street, after yielding to pedestrians and traffic. A steady yellow light means the signal is about to turn red. It does not mean speed up. If you can stop safely, come to a stop; if you are already within the intersection or too close to stop safely, proceed with caution and clear the intersection. A steady green light means you may go if the way is clear. Green does not guarantee right of way, so you must still yield to pedestrians, to vehicles still in the intersection, and to oncoming traffic when you turn left. Green arrows give protected movement in the direction shown.

entries.title: Flashing Signals and Arrows
entries.text: Flashing Signals and Arrows. A flashing red light works like a stop sign: come to a complete stop, yield as needed, and proceed when it is safe. A flashing yellow light means slow down and proceed with caution, watching for cross traffic and hazards. A flashing yellow arrow allows you to turn in that direction after yielding. Some traffic signals are dark because of a power failure or a malfunction. Treat a dark signal as an all-way stop: stop, then proceed in the order you arrived and yield to traffic already in the intersection. Do not assume the cross traffic has a red light when the signal is not working. Some intersections use a green arrow followed by a flashing yellow arrow for the same turn. The green arrow protects the turn, while the flashing yellow arrow means the turn is permitted but the driver must yield to oncoming traffic.

entries.title: White Pavement Markings
entries.text: White Pavement Markings. White lines separate traffic moving in the same direction. A single broken white line means you may change lanes when it is safe, while a solid white line discourages lane changes and a double solid white line means you should not cross it. White lines also mark the edge of the roadway and the right boundary of your lane. White markings outline crosswalks, stop lines, turn arrows, and the letters such as ONLY that show a lane is reserved for a specific movement. A solid white line across your lane before an intersection is the stop line where you must halt at a stop sign or red light. Painted arrows in white show which direction each lane must travel. If a lane is marked with a left-turn arrow, you must turn left from it rather than continuing straight, so choose your lane well before the intersection.

entries.title: Yellow Pavement Markings
entries.text: Yellow Pavement Markings. Yellow lines separate traffic moving in opposite directions. A broken yellow line means you may cross it to pass when it is safe and legal, while a solid yellow line means passing is discouraged and crossing it to pass is generally prohibited. A double solid yellow line means neither direction may cross to pass. When one side of a double yellow line is solid and the other is broken, the driver on the broken-line side may pass if it is safe, while the driver on the solid-line side may not. These lines show oncoming traffic where they can expect conflicting movements. A solid yellow line also marks the left edge of a divided highway or a center turn lane. A shared center lane bordered by solid and broken yellow lines is used for left turns in either direction, never for passing or normal travel.

entries.title: Special Markings
entries.text: Special Markings. Crosswalk markings warn drivers to expect pedestrians, whether or not they are currently visible. Even an unmarked crosswalk at an intersection is a legal crossing, so you must yield to pedestrians who are crossing there. Stop before the crosswalk so you do not block it. Railroad pavement markings, white transverse lines, and a yellow X with the letters RR warn of a railroad crossing ahead. A yellow X with the word ONLY may mark a lane reserved for a specific movement, and diamond symbols in a lane can indicate an HOV or special-use lane. White painted islands and chevron patterns show areas you should not drive on. Rumble strips, raised markers, and painted medians all guide traffic and separate opposing movements, especially where lanes shift such as at toll plazas or interchanges.

entries.title: Turning Right on Red
entries.text: Turning Right on Red. In Florida you may generally turn right on a steady red light after coming to a complete stop, unless a sign says no turn on red. Before turning, yield to pedestrians in the crosswalk and to any traffic approaching from the left, then complete the turn into the nearest lane when it is clear. Because a right turn on red is a permitted movement and not a protected one, the burden is on you to be sure the way is safe. Look left, then left again, and recheck the crosswalk, since a pedestrian or cyclist may be hidden by stopped vehicles. If a sign, a red arrow, or a steady red signal with a prohibitive sign is present, you must wait for a green light or a turn arrow. When in doubt, waiting is always acceptable and never a violation.

entries.title: Right of Way
entries.text: Right of Way. Right of way is not something you take; it is something you yield. This lesson explains who goes first at intersections, four-way stops, and crosswalks, and how to yield to emergency vehicles and pedestrians safely.

entries.title: How Intersections Work
entries.text: How Intersections Work. Right of way rules keep traffic moving in a predictable order when paths cross, and they exist to prevent confusion rather than to reward speed. The basic principle is that you yield to traffic already in the intersection and to traffic that has the legal priority, and you only proceed when it is safe. Signals, signs, and pavement markings usually tell you who goes first. Where none of them control the intersection, standard rules apply: yield to the vehicle on your right, and yield to traffic on the larger or main road when you are entering from a smaller one. A driver who has the right of way should still be ready to give it up to avoid a crash. The law may say one driver had priority, but that does not protect anyone from injury, so a defensive driver watches for others who may not yield.

entries.title: Four-Way Stops
entries.text: Four-Way Stops. At a four-way stop, the first vehicle to stop is the first to go. If two vehicles arrive at about the same time, the driver on the left yields to the driver on the right. If several vehicles arrive together, each moves in turn, usually in a clockwise order. The key is a full stop, not a rolling one. Once you have stopped, watch the other drivers to be sure they also intend to stop, because people sometimes misjudge who arrived first. Make eye contact or use a clear gesture when you are unsure. Do not wave another driver through if it would create confusion with other traffic. At a busy four-way stop, the safest approach is to take your turn predictably and to proceed only when the path across the intersection is truly clear.

entries.title: Uncontrolled Intersections
entries.text: Uncontrolled Intersections. An uncontrolled intersection has no signs or signals telling you who goes first. When two vehicles arrive at about the same time, the driver on the left must yield to the vehicle on the right. When you are entering a main road from a side road or driveway, you yield to traffic already on the main road. Uncontrolled intersections often appear in residential areas where sightlines are limited by parked cars, hedges, or corners. Approach them slowly enough that you can stop if a vehicle, pedestrian, or cyclist appears, and cover the brake so your reaction is immediate. A vehicle turning left must also yield to oncoming traffic that is going straight or turning right. Being the first to arrive does not give a left-turning driver permission to cut across approaching traffic before it is safe.

entries.title: Pedestrians and Crosswalks
entries.text: Pedestrians and Crosswalks. Pedestrians generally have the right of way in crosswalks and at intersections, whether or not the crosswalk is painted. You must yield and often must stop for a pedestrian who is in your lane or crossing toward it, and you should not pass a vehicle that has stopped for a pedestrian. Blind pedestrians may use a white cane or a guide dog, and they always have the right of way at a crosswalk even outside of one in some situations. Give them plenty of space and time, and never honk to hurry a pedestrian, since that can cause someone to stumble. A pedestrian who jaywalks, meaning crossing outside a crosswalk where there are signals, commits a violation, but drivers should still avoid hitting anyone. Yielding promptly avoids an emergency and keeps everyone safer, regardless of who technically has priority.

entries.title: Emergency and Special Vehicles
entries.text: Emergency and Special Vehicles. When an emergency vehicle approaches with lights and a siren, pull over to the right edge of the road and stop until it passes. Do not block an intersection: if you are in one, clear it first and then pull over. If the emergency vehicle is on the other side of a divided highway, you may generally continue. After an emergency vehicle passes, check carefully before pulling back into traffic, since other emergency vehicles may be following. Never chase or follow an emergency vehicle closely to take advantage of the gap it creates. You must also yield to school buses with flashing red lights and to vehicles such as postal trucks, garbage trucks, and buses that are making frequent stops. Give them room to stop and restart, and never pass a stopped school bus that is loading or unloading children.

entries.title: Yielding While Turning and Merging
entries.text: Yielding While Turning and Merging. Drivers who are turning generally yield to traffic that is not turning. A left-turning driver waits for oncoming vehicles going straight or turning right, and a driver entering a road from a driveway or parking lot yields to all traffic on the road. When you merge from an on-ramp onto a highway, you yield to traffic already on the highway and use the ramp to match its speed. When lanes merge into one, drivers in the ending lane yield to those in the continuing lane, though cooperative drivers often take turns. Cyclists and motorcyclists have the same rights and responsibilities as other drivers, so yield to them as you would to a car. Give them a full lane when possible and never squeeze past them, since they need room to avoid hazards like potholes and debris.

entries.title: Speed & Following Distance
entries.text: Speed & Following Distance. Speed limits set a maximum for good conditions, not a guarantee of safety. This lesson covers Florida default speed limits, the two-second following rule, and how speed affects your stopping distance in real traffic.

entries.title: Florida Default Speed Limits
entries.text: Florida Default Speed Limits. When no sign is posted, Florida sets default speed limits you are expected to know. The limit is generally 30 mph in a business or residential district, 55 mph on a two-lane undivided road outside an urban area, and up to 70 mph where posted on interstate and limited-access highways. These defaults apply only where no lower or higher limit is posted, and a posted sign always governs the specific stretch of road. Many local streets and some state roads have their own posted limits that fit local conditions, and those signs must be followed. A speed limit is the maximum for ideal conditions, and it is never a required speed. Driving significantly slower than surrounding traffic can also be unsafe, but you are always allowed to go slower when conditions demand it, and you must never exceed the posted maximum.

entries.title: Posted Limits and the Basic Speed Law
entries.text: Posted Limits and the Basic Speed Law. The basic speed law means you must always drive at a speed that is safe for the current conditions, even if that speed is lower than the posted limit. Rain, fog, darkness, heavy traffic, and road construction are all reasons to slow below the maximum. The posted limit does not protect you from a citation if you are driving too fast for conditions. If an officer judges your speed unsafe for the situation, you can be cited even while technically below the posted number, because safety, not the sign alone, defines a reasonable speed. Speed limits are often reduced near schools, parks, and intersections where more people are likely to be near the road. Watch for yellow warning signs and extra speed limit signs that signal a change is coming, and slow before you reach the point where the new limit applies.

entries.title: Following Distance
entries.text: Following Distance. A safe following distance gives you time to react to the car ahead without relying on their brake lights. Use the two-second rule as a minimum in good conditions: pick a fixed object ahead, and when the car in front passes it, count two seconds before you reach it. If you reach it sooner, you are following too closely. Increase the count to three, four, or more seconds when you are behind a large truck, on a wet or slippery road, in heavy traffic, at night, or when visibility is reduced. Tailgating removes your reaction time and is a leading cause of rear-end crashes. When someone follows you too closely, do not brake suddenly to teach them a lesson. Instead, increase the space ahead of you so you can slow gradually, and let the impatient driver pass when it is safe.

entries.title: Stopping Distance
entries.text: Stopping Distance. Stopping distance is the sum of your reaction distance and your braking distance. Reaction distance is how far you travel during the moment before you actually brake, and braking distance is how far the car takes to stop once the brakes engage. Both grow as speed increases. Because braking distance increases with the square of your speed, going twice as fast can take about four times the distance to stop. This is why speeding near pedestrians, bicyclists, or a stopped bus is so dangerous: you simply cannot stop in time if someone steps out. Wet roads, worn tires, and heavy loads all lengthen braking distance. In the rain, allow extra following space and slow below the posted limit so your total stopping distance fits within the room you actually have.

entries.title: School, Work, and Residential Zones
entries.text: School, Work, and Residential Zones. School zones often have a much lower speed limit, commonly around 20 mph, and these limits usually apply when children are present or when the lights are flashing. Slow down before you reach the school and watch for crossing guards and children who may move unpredictably. Work zones usually post temporary speed limits that may be lower than the normal limit, and fines can be higher for speeding there. Residential and business districts generally have a 30 mph default limit, but parked cars, driveways, and pedestrians mean you should stay alert and ready to slow. In any of these zones, the goal is not just to match the number but to match the level of risk. Where there are people near the road, driving the posted limit at night or in rain may still be too fast, so use the basic speed law to guide your choice.

entries.title: Turning, Lanes & Parking
entries.text: Turning, Lanes & Parking. Clear turns, safe lane changes, and correct parking depend on signaling early and choosing the right lane. This lesson explains turn rules, U-turns, lane discipline, and how to park legally and safely at a curb.

entries.title: Signaling Your Intentions
entries.text: Signaling Your Intentions. Turn signals let other drivers and pedestrians know what you plan to do, and Florida law requires you to signal before turning or changing lanes. Signal at least 100 feet before a turn in normal city driving, and well in advance on highways so others have time to react. A signal is a promise, so use it only when you are actually going to make the movement. Signaling far ahead and then not turning confuses other drivers, and leaving a signal on by accident can cause someone to pull out in front of you. Cancel your signal after completing the turn or lane change, and if a vehicle is in your blind spot, continue signaling until it is safe to move. Good signaling is a habit that prevents the most common kinds of urban crashes.

entries.title: Right and Left Turns
entries.text: Right and Left Turns. For a right turn, come close to the right curb or edge of the road, signal early, and turn into the nearest lane of the street you are entering. For a left turn, begin from the leftmost legal lane or a dedicated left-turn lane, then turn into the lane closest to the center line of the new road. When two vehicles turn from opposite directions into a multi-lane road, they may generally turn into different lanes at the same time, but each must stay within its own path. Staying in your own lane avoids side-swiping and keeps the turn predictable for everyone. Turning from the wrong lane, or turning wide into the far lane, is a common cause of intersection crashes. Choose your lane early, watch for pedestrians and cyclists in the crosswalk, and complete the turn without drifting across lane lines.

entries.title: U-Turns
entries.text: U-Turns. A U-turn lets you reverse direction, and in Florida it is generally allowed unless a sign prohibits it or it is unsafe. You may not make a U-turn where you cannot see clearly, in the middle of a curve or hill, or in a business district where signs forbid it. Before making a U-turn, signal, check for oncoming traffic, and make sure you can complete the turn without interfering with any other vehicle or pedestrian. Never make a U-turn across a divided highway except at an opening or crossover designed for that purpose. A U-turn that forces other drivers to brake or swerve is illegal even if no sign forbids it, because it is unsafe. When you are unsure whether a U-turn is allowed, choose a legal intersection or turn-around point instead.

entries.title: Changing Lanes
entries.text: Changing Lanes. Lane changes should be smooth and deliberate, never sudden. Check your mirrors, signal, then do a quick head check over your shoulder to cover the blind spot that mirrors do not show. Move only when you can see that the adjacent lane is clear and there is enough space. Maintain your speed or adjust it slightly to match traffic during the change, and never cut off a vehicle that is already there. Weaving in and out of traffic to gain a few car lengths is risky and gains almost nothing on a typical trip. Keep to the right except when passing or preparing for a left turn, and use the correct lane for your direction of travel. On a multi-lane road, staying in one lane and driving predictably is safer than constant lane changes.

entries.title: Parking and Curbs
entries.text: Parking and Curbs. When parking on a public road, stop with your vehicle close to and parallel with the curb, and make sure you do not block driveways, fire hydrants, or crosswalks. Set the parking brake, turn off the engine, and remove the key before leaving the vehicle. On a two-way street, park with the right wheels within a foot of the curb. When parking facing downhill, turn your front wheels toward the curb so the car rolls into the curb if the brake fails; facing uphill with a curb, turn the wheels away from the curb. Before opening your door, check mirrors and look over your shoulder for cyclists and passing cars. A door opened into the path of a cyclist is a common and serious crash, so use the hand that is away from the door to open it, forcing your body to turn and look back.

entries.title: Where Parking Is Prohibited
entries.text: Where Parking Is Prohibited. You may not park where a sign or curb marking forbids it, and you must not park within an intersection, on a crosswalk, or on a sidewalk. Parking is also prohibited in front of a driveway, within 15 feet of a fire hydrant, and near stop signs or traffic signals where it would block the view. Do not park on a bridge, in a tunnel, or on the traveled portion of a highway unless it is an emergency. On a hill, in a curve, or anywhere your vehicle blocks other drivers from seeing traffic, parking is both illegal and dangerous. Parking in a space reserved for people with disabilities without a proper permit can bring a substantial fine, and these spaces are enforced closely. Always check nearby signs and curb paint, since restrictions such as no parking during certain hours are common in business districts.

entries.title: Defensive Driving & Safety
entries.text: Defensive Driving & Safety. Defensive driving means protecting yourself even when other road users make mistakes. This lesson covers scanning, keeping a space cushion, using seat belts and child restraints, avoiding distractions, and sharing the road with cyclists, motorcycles, and large trucks.

entries.title: Scanning and the Space Cushion
entries.text: Scanning and the Space Cushion. Defensive driving starts with looking far ahead, roughly 12 to 15 seconds down the road, so you see problems before they reach you. Scan your mirrors regularly and keep your eyes moving so you always know what is beside and behind you as well as ahead. A space cushion is the area you keep clear around your vehicle so you have time and room to react. Leave space ahead, avoid riding in another driver blind spot, and do not box yourself in next to large vehicles or in the middle of a tight group of cars. The most important part of the space cushion is ahead of you, because that is where you need room to slow down. If you find yourself running out of following distance, ease off the accelerator early rather than waiting to brake hard.

entries.title: Seat Belts and Child Restraints
entries.text: Seat Belts and Child Restraints. Florida law requires seat belts to be worn, and the safest position is with the lap belt low across your hips and the shoulder belt over your chest, never under your arm or behind your back. Wearing a seat belt greatly reduces the chance of being killed or seriously injured in a crash. Children under 4 years old must be secured in a federally approved child restraint, and older children should use a booster seat until the seat belt fits them properly. The safest place for a young child is generally the rear seat, and a rear-facing seat must never be placed in front of an active air bag. The driver is responsible for making sure passengers under 18 are properly restrained. Before starting the car, check that everyone is buckled and that children are in the correct seat for their age and size.

entries.title: Distracted Driving
entries.text: Distracted Driving. Distraction takes your eyes, hands, or mind away from driving, and the most dangerous distractions do all three at once. Texting combines looking, touching, and thinking about something other than the road, which is why it is so risky and is prohibited while driving in Florida. Other common distractions include eating, adjusting the radio or navigation, reaching for an object, grooming, and interacting with passengers or pets. Even a few seconds of inattention at highway speed covers the length of a football field before you react. Manage distraction before it starts: set your navigation and music before you drive, secure pets and loose items, and let calls go to voicemail. If you must handle something, pull over safely rather than dividing your attention at the wheel.

entries.title: Sharing the Road
entries.text: Sharing the Road. Cyclists have the same rights and duties as drivers, and they often need the whole lane to avoid hazards. Pass them only when you can give at least three feet and there is no oncoming traffic, and watch for them when you turn or open a door, since they may be hidden behind parked cars. Motorcycles are smaller and harder to see, so look twice before turning or changing lanes, especially at intersections. Never share a lane with a motorcycle, and allow them a full lane as you would a car. Pedestrians, people on scooters, and children are also part of traffic. Slow down in areas where people gather, give them room, and expect that a person on foot may not see or hear you, particularly at dusk or in rain.

entries.title: Sharing the Road with Large Trucks
entries.text: Sharing the Road with Large Trucks. Large trucks and buses take much longer to stop and need more room to turn, so never cut in front of one and then brake. They also have large blind spots, often called no-zones, on both sides, directly behind, and in front, so if you cannot see the driver in the mirror, the driver cannot see you. Trucks swing wide when turning, which means they may move toward the opposite lane before completing a turn. Do not squeeze into the space beside a turning truck, and give them room to complete the turn safely. When passing a large vehicle, pass on the left when possible, move through the blind spot promptly, and do not linger alongside. After passing, wait until you can see the front of the truck in your mirror before you return to its lane.

entries.title: Driving in Bad Weather
entries.text: Driving in Bad Weather. Rain is common in Florida and it makes the road slippery, especially in the first minutes when oil and dust have not yet washed away. Slow down, increase your following distance, and turn on your headlights so others can see you, even in daytime rain. Hydroplaning happens when your tires ride on a thin film of water and you lose contact with the road. If you feel the steering go light, ease off the accelerator, avoid hard braking, and keep the wheel steady until the tires grip again. In fog, use low-beam headlights and slow down, and never stop on the traveled part of the road. Thunderstorms and flooding can make water deep enough to stall or sweep away a car, so never drive into water covering the road when you cannot see how deep it is.

entries.title: Alcohol, Drugs & Impairment
entries.text: Alcohol, Drugs & Impairment. Alcohol and drugs slow your judgment, reactions, and coordination long before you feel drunk. This lesson explains Florida blood alcohol limits, zero tolerance for drivers under 21, how other substances impair driving, and the legal consequences of impaired driving.

entries.title: How Alcohol Affects Driving
entries.text: How Alcohol Affects Driving. Alcohol is a depressant that slows the brain and nervous system, so it weakens the very skills driving depends on. It reduces your ability to judge speed and distance, shortens your attention span, and slows your reaction time, all before you feel intoxicated. The first skills to go are judgment and self-control, which is why an impaired driver often feels more confident while actually driving worse. Alcohol also reduces vision, especially at night and in judging how far away lights and other cars are. There is no safe amount of alcohol for driving. Even one or two drinks can affect your reactions, and combining alcohol with fatigue or medicine makes the impairment worse. The only reliable way to avoid alcohol impairment is not to drink before driving.

entries.title: Legal BAC Limits
entries.text: Legal BAC Limits. In Florida it is illegal to drive with a blood alcohol concentration of 0.08 or higher for drivers 21 and older. Being under the limit does not mean you are safe or legal, because you can still be convicted of DUI if your normal faculties are impaired. Drivers under 21 are held to zero tolerance, which means a blood or breath alcohol level of 0.02 or higher is a violation. Because young drivers are less experienced and more affected by small amounts of alcohol, this limit is intentionally very low. Commercial drivers are also held to a lower standard, generally 0.04, because the size and weight of their vehicles make impairment far more dangerous. Knowing the limits helps, but the safest plan is always to separate drinking from driving entirely.

entries.title: Zero Tolerance for Under 21
entries.text: Zero Tolerance for Under 21. Florida enforces zero tolerance for drivers under 21, and the consequences begin with the first offense. A young driver found with a blood or breath alcohol level of 0.02 or higher can have the license suspended, even if the amount is small and even if the driver does not feel impaired. Zero tolerance exists because alcohol affects young drivers more and because early habits shape lifelong behavior. Mixing alcohol with inexperience means longer reaction times, poorer judgment, and a much higher crash risk. If you are under 21, the safest and simplest rule is not to drink at all before getting behind the wheel. If you have been drinking, call for a ride, use a designated driver, or stay where you are rather than driving.

entries.title: Other Drugs and Medications
entries.text: Other Drugs and Medications. Drugs other than alcohol can impair driving just as seriously, and this includes both illegal drugs and prescription or over-the-counter medicines. Marijuana, for example, can slow reactions, reduce coordination, and distort the sense of time and distance. Many common medicines, such as antihistamines, sleep aids, and pain relievers, cause drowsiness or slow reactions, and their warnings often advise against driving. Combining any central nervous system medicine with alcohol multiplies the effect far beyond each one alone. In Florida, driving under the influence of any substance, including legally prescribed medicine, is illegal when it impairs your normal faculties. Always read the label, ask your doctor or pharmacist about driving, and do not drive if a medicine makes you drowsy or unfocused.

entries.title: Consequences of DUI
entries.text: Consequences of DUI. A DUI conviction in Florida carries serious costs, and the penalties grow with each offense. They can include fines, license suspension or revocation, jail time, required education or treatment programs, and the installation of an ignition interlock device on your vehicle. Beyond the legal penalties, a DUI affects your insurance rates, can cost you a job or a professional license, and stays on your record for years. If someone is injured or killed, the consequences become far more severe, including prison and lifelong responsibility. You can be charged with DUI even if you are under the legal BAC limit or refuse the breath test. Florida law also allows enhanced penalties in some cases, such as a very high BAC or having a child in the vehicle, so the safest choice is always to not drive after drinking or using impairing substances.

entries.title: Recognizing Impairment
entries.text: Recognizing Impairment. Because alcohol weakens your own judgment first, you are the least reliable judge of your own fitness to drive after drinking. Never rely on feeling fine; use a plan made before you drink, such as a designated driver, a rideshare, or staying overnight. Warning signs of impairment in other drivers include weaving, drifting, sudden braking, driving very slowly, and ignoring signals. If you suspect an impaired driver, keep your distance, do not try to stop them yourself, and call law enforcement with a description and location. Fatigue produces effects similar to alcohol, including slow reactions and lapses in attention. Drowsy driving is dangerous on its own, so do not treat caffeine or an open window as a substitute for rest. If you are sleepy, pull over and rest.

entries.title: Emergencies & Special Situations
entries.text: Emergencies & Special Situations. Emergencies demand calm, correct reactions rather than panic. This lesson covers brake failure, tire blowouts, skids, railroad crossings, and weather hazards, so you know what to do before a sudden problem happens.

entries.title: Brake Failure
entries.text: Brake Failure. If your brakes fail, stay calm and pump the brake pedal firmly and repeatedly, because this can build up pressure and restore some braking. Downshift to a lower gear so the engine helps slow the car, and apply the parking brake gradually rather than all at once. Look for an escape route, such as an open shoulder, an uphill grade, or a gravel area that will slow you. If you must stop quickly, you can rub the wheels against a curb or guardrail to shed speed, but do it gently to avoid losing control or spinning. Avoid turning off the engine while moving, because you would lose power steering and possibly the ability to steer. Sound your horn and flash your lights to warn others, and only use the parking brake fully once you are prepared for a sudden stop.

entries.title: Tire Blowouts
entries.text: Tire Blowouts. When a tire blows out, the car may pull to the side of the failed tire and the steering may jerk. Grip the wheel firmly with both hands, keep the car going straight, and ease off the accelerator slowly instead of braking hard. Do not slam on the brakes, because that can make the car swerve or roll, especially if the failure is at the front. Let the car slow gradually, then pull off the road to a safe place well away from traffic before you change the tire or call for help. If a front tire blows, the pull will be stronger, so keep the wheel straight and steer gently as you slow. Turn on your hazard lights as soon as you can to warn drivers behind you that you are slowing.

entries.title: Skids
entries.text: Skids. A skid happens when the tires lose grip, often on a wet road, ice, sand, or during hard braking. If your rear wheels skid, steer gently in the direction you want the front of the car to go, and ease off the accelerator and brakes so the tires can regain traction. If your front wheels skid, you lose steering and the car goes straight even as you turn the wheel. Ease off the accelerator and brakes to let the front tires grip again, then steer where you want to go. In both cases, look and steer where you want the car to go, not at what you fear hitting. Preventing a skid is easier than fixing one. Slow down before curves and wet surfaces, brake gently, and avoid sudden steering, which is what breaks the grip in the first place. On Florida roads, the first rain after a dry spell is especially slippery.

entries.title: Railroad Crossings
entries.text: Railroad Crossings. Railroad crossings require you to slow down and look both ways, because a train cannot stop quickly and always has the right of way. If warning lights are flashing, a gate is lowering, or you can see or hear a train, stop well before the tracks and wait. Never stop on the tracks or start across unless you are sure you can clear the entire crossing, including any vehicle in front of you. If your vehicle stalls on the tracks, get everyone out and away from the tracks immediately, then call for help rather than trying to restart the car. Trains can be closer and moving faster than they appear, and at night a train may be silent until it is very near. At a crossing with no gates or lights, stop, look both ways, and listen before you proceed, and never try to beat a train.

entries.title: Breakdowns and Road Hazards
entries.text: Breakdowns and Road Hazards. If your vehicle breaks down, get it as far off the traveled lane as you can and onto the shoulder or a safe area. Turn on your hazard lights, raise the hood if it is safe, and stay in the vehicle with your seat belt on if traffic makes standing outside dangerous. Place warning triangles or reflectors behind your car when it is safe and you have them, especially on a highway, so approaching drivers have time to change lanes. When help is far away, call for roadside assistance and give a clear description of your location using mile markers. Debris, potholes, and animals are common roadway hazards. Do not swerve sharply at the last second, since that can cause a worse crash than the hazard itself; slow down in a controlled way and steer around only when you have checked that the space beside you is clear.

entries.title: Severe Weather
entries.text: Severe Weather. Florida is known for sudden downpours, lightning, and tropical storms. When heavy rain reduces visibility, slow down, use your headlights, and increase your following distance, and if you cannot see well, pull off the road in a safe place rather than continuing blindly. If you are caught in strong wind or a tornado warning, do not try to outrun it in the car. Get out of the vehicle and take shelter in a sturdy building, or if none is available, lie in a low ditch and protect your head, because a vehicle can be blown over. Never drive through moving flood water, because even shallow water can hide a washed-out road or sweep a car away. Water deep enough to cover the road is a reason to stop and turn around, not to test how far you can go.

entries.title: Highways & Passing
entries.text: Highways & Passing. Highways and interstates move traffic fast, which rewards smooth, predictable driving. This lesson explains how to enter and exit highways, when passing is legal and safe, and how to drive on limited-access roads.

entries.title: Entering a Highway
entries.text: Entering a Highway. An on-ramp is designed to let you build up speed so you can merge into highway traffic at a similar speed. Use the full length of the ramp to accelerate, check your mirrors, and look over your shoulder for a gap before you merge. Traffic already on the highway has the right of way, so you must yield and find a safe opening rather than expecting others to move over. If the ramp ends and traffic is heavy, you may need to slow and adjust, but you must still merge without forcing others to brake. Once you are on the highway, settle into a steady speed and keep to the right except when passing. Entering at too low a speed creates a dangerous speed difference, and stopping at the end of a ramp is one of the riskiest mistakes on highways.

entries.title: Matching Speed and Choosing a Lane
entries.text: Matching Speed and Choosing a Lane. Merging safely means matching the speed of traffic in the lane you are joining, not the speed of the ramp you just left. Look for a gap that is large enough to fit your vehicle plus a safety margin, then move in smoothly rather than abruptly. On a highway with several lanes, the right lane is generally for slower traffic and vehicles entering and leaving, while the left lanes are for faster traffic and passing. The far-left paved shoulder is not a driving lane, and it is only for emergencies or disabled vehicles. On many Florida freeways, the leftmost lane is a managed express lane. These lanes may require a transponder and a toll, and drivers who enter them without paying can be fined. Plan your lane changes early and never cross the solid lines that separate express lanes from general lanes.

entries.title: Rules for Passing
entries.text: Rules for Passing. Passing is normally done on the left, and you must signal before you pull out, check that the way is clear, and return to the original lane only when you can see the passed vehicle in your mirror. On a multi-lane road, the vehicle being passed should not speed up to block you. When you pass a vehicle, accelerate smoothly and move through the other driver blind spot without lingering, then signal and return to the lane at a safe distance. Maintain your speed during the pass so the maneuver is quick and predictable. Passing is prohibited where it would be unsafe, such as on a curve, at the crest of a hill, at a railroad crossing, or at an intersection, and wherever a solid yellow line, a no-passing sign, or a pennant marks the zone. In these places you simply wait until you reach a legal passing area.

entries.title: When Not to Pass
entries.text: When Not to Pass. Never pass when you cannot see far enough ahead to complete the maneuver safely, because an oncoming vehicle could appear with no time to react. Do not pass when approaching a hill crest, a curve, a bridge, a tunnel, or a railroad crossing where your view is blocked. Do not pass at intersections or where a solid line, a sign, or a pennant forbids it. Do not pass a vehicle that has stopped at a crosswalk, a school bus loading or unloading children, or an emergency vehicle that is responding to a call. Whenever you are unsure whether passing is safe or legal, wait. The few seconds you might save are not worth the risk of a head-on crash, which is among the most serious kinds of collisions on two-lane roads.

entries.title: Being Passed
entries.text: Being Passed. When another driver wants to pass you, keep to the right, hold your speed steady, and give them room to complete the pass. Do not speed up, because that keeps the passing driver alongside you longer and increases the danger for both of you. If you see a vehicle that has started to pass and cannot finish safely, slowing down slightly can help it return to the lane sooner. Being predictable is more valuable than being right, and courtesy prevents crashes. The same rules apply to cyclists and motorcyclists you are passing: give them enough space, and never crowd them into the edge of the road. Move over a lane when possible to give anyone you pass a comfortable margin.

entries.title: Exiting the Highway
entries.text: Exiting the Highway. Plan your exit well ahead by watching the guide signs and moving into the correct lane early. Signal before the exit, slow down after you are on the deceleration ramp rather than in the travel lane, and obey the advisory speed posted for the curve of the ramp. Do not cross a gore area, which is the triangular zone marked with white lines, and do not back up if you miss the exit. Continue to the next exit and turn around safely, because backing up on a highway is both illegal and extremely dangerous. If you are exiting from an express or toll lane, make sure you know the rules for that lane and pay as required. Missing a toll can lead to a violation notice, and trying to squeeze across the barriers at the last moment risks a serious crash.

entries.title: Florida Driving Laws
entries.text: Florida Driving Laws. Florida has its own driving laws that go beyond the general rules of the road. This lesson covers the Move Over law, school bus and school zone rules, the cell phone law, license classes, mandatory insurance, and the point system.

entries.title: The Move Over Law
entries.text: The Move Over Law. Florida requires drivers to move over for emergency and service vehicles stopped on the side of the road with their lights on, such as law enforcement, fire, ambulance, tow trucks, and utility vehicles. If you are on a road with two or more lanes in your direction, move into a lane that is not next to the stopped vehicle. When you cannot move over safely because of traffic or the road layout, you must slow down to at least 20 mph below the posted speed limit and pass with care. The law applies on both divided and undivided roads, and it also covers sanitation and utility vehicles displaying warning lights. The reason is simple: officers, tow operators, and utility workers are often standing on the shoulder with traffic rushing past. Moving over or slowing down gives them the space and time they need to work safely, and failing to do so can lead to a citation.

entries.title: School Buses and School Zones
entries.text: School Buses and School Zones. When a school bus stops with its red lights flashing and its stop arm extended, you must stop in both directions and wait until the lights stop flashing, unless you are on a divided highway separated by a raised median or barrier. On such a divided highway, only traffic on the same side of the median as the bus must stop. You must remain stopped until the red lights stop flashing and the stop arm is withdrawn, even if no children are visible. Passing a stopped school bus with active red lights is a serious violation because children may cross the road unexpectedly. School zones generally have a reduced speed limit, commonly around 20 mph, that applies when children are present or when the zone lights are flashing. Slow down before the zone begins and watch for crossing guards, since the goal is to protect children who may move without warning.

entries.title: Cell Phones and Texting
entries.text: Cell Phones and Texting. Florida law prohibits texting while driving as a primary offense, which means an officer can stop you for it without another reason. Typing, reading, and sending messages all count, and the law exists because texting takes your eyes, hands, and mind off the road. The use of a handheld phone is prohibited in school zones and work zones, where you must put the device down and use only hands-free technology if it is allowed. In these areas, holding a phone while driving can lead to a citation even if you are not texting. Using a phone when your full attention is needed is dangerous everywhere, even where it is technically permitted, such as a hands-free call. The safest habit is to set up navigation and messages before you drive and to leave the phone out of reach.

entries.title: License Classes
entries.text: License Classes. Florida issues driver licenses by class, and the standard one for most drivers is the Class E license, which allows you to drive a regular passenger car, a pickup, and similar non-commercial vehicles. A learner license, often called a Class E learner license, lets a beginner practice while driving with a supervising licensed driver who is at least 21. Drivers who need to operate larger or commercial vehicles must hold the appropriate commercial license, and motorcycle riders generally need a motorcycle endorsement on their license. Each class has its own tests and requirements. A Florida driver must carry a valid license while driving and show it when requested by law enforcement. Losing a license through suspension or revocation means you may not drive until the state restores it, and driving while suspended carries serious penalties.

entries.title: Insurance and No-Fault
entries.text: Insurance and No-Fault. Florida is a no-fault insurance state, which means that after a crash your own insurance pays for certain of your injuries first, regardless of who caused the crash. Drivers must carry Personal Injury Protection, which covers a portion of medical costs and lost income, and Property Damage Liability for damage to others property. You must have valid insurance to register a vehicle and to drive legally, and driving without it can lead to fines, suspension of your license and registration, and higher costs later. Proof of coverage is required in many situations, including when you register or renew a vehicle. No-fault does not mean no one is responsible for unsafe driving. A seriously injured person may still pursue a claim against the driver who caused the crash, and a driver whose unsafe actions caused harm can face both civil and criminal consequences.

entries.title: The Point System
entries.text: The Point System. Florida uses a point system to track traffic violations, and points are added to your driving record for convictions such as speeding and running a red light. The number of points depends on the type and severity of the violation, and more serious violations carry more points. If you accumulate too many points in a period of time, your license can be suspended. For example, a driver who reaches 12 points within 12 months generally faces a suspension, and higher totals over longer periods bring longer suspensions. The exact thresholds are set by Florida law and your driving record can be checked with the state. Points stay on your record for a set time and can raise your insurance costs. Some drivers can reduce points by completing an approved driving course, but this option is limited and does not erase serious violations. Safe driving is the only way to keep a clean record.

entries.title: Other Florida Rules to Know
entries.text: Other Florida Rules to Know. Florida permits a right turn on a steady red light after a complete stop unless a sign prohibits it, and it also requires seat belts and federally approved child restraints for young children. These rules combine with the general laws of the road you have already learned. A driver must stop for a pedestrian in a crosswalk, obey a flagger in a work zone, and use headlights in rain and from sunset to sunrise. Driving while your license is suspended, reckless driving, and street racing are all serious offenses with severe penalties. Local governments may add their own rules, so always follow posted signs, even if they differ from what you learned elsewhere. Knowing both the state law and the local sign is part of being a responsible Florida driver, and when a sign and a habit conflict, the sign controls.

entries.title: Stop
entries.text: Stop. Come to a complete stop at the stop line or before entering the crosswalk, then proceed only when it is safe and you have the right of way.. You will see it at intersections, at the end of highway exit ramps and before railroad crossings.

entries.title: Yield
entries.text: Yield. Slow down and let other vehicles, bicyclists and pedestrians go first. Stop if necessary. You must give the right of way.. Found at intersections and at freeway on-ramps where traffic on the main road has priority.

entries.title: Do Not Enter
entries.text: Do Not Enter. Do not drive past this sign. The road or lane ahead is closed to traffic coming from your direction.. Posted at wrong-way entrances to divided highways, on one-way streets and at restricted exits.

entries.title: No U-Turn
entries.text: No U-Turn. U-turns are not allowed at this location.. Used at intersections, medians and driveways where turning around would be unsafe or would disrupt traffic.

entries.title: Speed Limit
entries.text: Speed Limit. Shows the maximum legal speed, in miles per hour, that you may drive under good conditions.. Posted along streets and highways. Where no limit is posted, the limits set by Florida law apply.

entries.title: No Parking
entries.text: No Parking. Parking is not allowed at any time along the section of roadway controlled by this sign.. Found on city streets and near fire hydrants, bus stops and driveways.

entries.title: One Way
entries.text: One Way. Traffic on this street or roadway moves in only one direction, shown by the arrow.. Posted at intersections with one-way streets and along divided roadways.

entries.title: Wrong Way
entries.text: Wrong Way. You are entering a roadway against the flow of traffic. Turn around as soon as it is safe to do so.. Mounted facing drivers who are about to enter a divided highway or one-way street the wrong way.

entries.title: Keep Right
entries.text: Keep Right. Pass to the right of a median, island or obstacle. Do not go to the left of it.. Placed on medians and islands that traffic can pass on only one side.

entries.title: No Left Turn
entries.text: No Left Turn. Left turns are not allowed at this intersection.. Used where left turns would block traffic or create a safety hazard.

entries.title: Do Not Pass
entries.text: Do Not Pass. Do not pass other vehicles on this section of road. Stay in your lane and wait until passing is allowed.. Used on two-lane roads with curves, hills or limited sight distance where passing is unsafe.

entries.title: Curve Ahead
entries.text: Curve Ahead. A curve is ahead. Slow down before the curve and obey the safe speed.. Placed before curves where the safe speed is lower than the posted limit.

entries.title: Intersection Ahead
entries.text: Intersection Ahead. A four-way intersection is ahead. Watch for crossing and turning traffic.. Posted on rural roads and streets where drivers may not expect a crossroad.

entries.title: Pedestrian Crossing
entries.text: Pedestrian Crossing. Pedestrians may be crossing the road ahead. Slow down and be ready to stop.. Found near schools, parks, shopping areas and other places where people cross.

entries.title: Deer Crossing
entries.text: Deer Crossing. Deer often cross the road in this area. Slow down, especially at dawn and dusk.. Placed on rural roads and highways near wooded areas where deer are common.

entries.title: Traffic Signal Ahead
entries.text: Traffic Signal Ahead. A traffic signal is ahead. Be ready to stop if the light turns red.. Placed before signals that drivers may not see in time, such as after a hill or a curve.

entries.title: Slippery When Wet
entries.text: Slippery When Wet. The road may be slippery when wet. Slow down and avoid sudden braking or turning in the rain.. Used on bridges, overpasses and pavement that loses traction when wet.

entries.title: Railroad Crossing Ahead
entries.text: Railroad Crossing Ahead. A railroad crossing is ahead. Slow down, look and listen, and be ready to stop.. Placed in advance of railroad crossings that do not have gates or flashing lights.

entries.title: Two-Way Traffic
entries.text: Two-Way Traffic. Two-way traffic is ahead. Keep right and do not drive in the oncoming lane.. Used where a one-way road becomes two-way or after a divided highway ends.

entries.title: Merge
entries.text: Merge. Another lane of traffic will merge into yours. Adjust your speed and let merging vehicles in.. Posted where an on-ramp or side road joins the roadway you are on.

entries.title: Lane Ends
entries.text: Lane Ends. A lane ends ahead. Merge into the lane that continues and do not cut off other drivers.. Used where a lane is dropped, such as before a merge area or a bridge.

entries.title: Interstate Shield
entries.text: Interstate Shield. Identifies an Interstate highway and its route number. Interstates are the fastest, limited-access highways.. Posted on guide signs, trailblazers and markers along the Interstate system.

entries.title: Exit Only
entries.text: Exit Only. This lane goes only to the exit. If you want to continue straight, move to another lane.. Placed over or beside lanes that leave the highway at an exit ramp.

entries.title: Mile Marker
entries.text: Mile Marker. Shows the number of miles from where the road begins in the state. It helps you and emergency services find your location.. Placed at intervals along highways so drivers can report their location after a breakdown.

entries.title: Services
entries.text: Services. Shows that services such as gas, food or lodging are available at the next exit.. Posted before exits that have the services shown on the sign.

entries.title: School Zone
entries.text: School Zone. Marks the beginning of a school zone. Obey the posted school speed limit while the lights flash or students are present.. Placed at the entrance to areas around schools where children may be near the road.

entries.title: School Crossing
entries.text: School Crossing. Children are crossing the road here. Stop for the crossing guard and for students in the crosswalk.. Posted at and near school crossings where children walk to and from school.

entries.title: Road Work Ahead
entries.text: Road Work Ahead. Road work is ahead. Slow down, watch for workers and equipment, and be ready to stop.. Placed in advance of construction, maintenance and utility work on the roadway.

entries.title: Flagger Ahead
entries.text: Flagger Ahead. A flagger controls traffic ahead. Follow the flagger signals and stop or go when directed.. Used in work zones where traffic must take turns through a single open lane.

entries.title: Detour
entries.text: Detour. The road ahead is closed. Follow this route to go around the closed area.. Posted along the temporary route that takes traffic around a closed road or work zone.

entries.title: Señales de tránsito
entries.text: Señales de tránsito. Las señales de tránsito comunican reglas, peligros e indicaciones mediante formas y colores consistentes. Esta lección te enseña a reconocer señales reglamentarias, preventivas, informativas y de obras con rapidez para que reacciones antes de que el peligro te alcance.

entries.title: Formas y colores
entries.text: Formas y colores. Las señales de tránsito en Florida siguen estándares nacionales, por lo que su forma y su color transmiten el mensaje general antes de que leas una sola palabra. Un octágono siempre es una señal de ALTO, y un triángulo apuntando hacia abajo siempre es una señal de CEDA EL PASO. Un rectángulo vertical suele ser reglamentario, mientras que un rectángulo horizontal suele ser informativo. Un rombo te advierte que hay un peligro adelante, y una forma de banderín marca el inicio de una zona donde no se puede adelantar. El color transmite tanto significado como la forma. El rojo significa alto o prohibición, y el amarillo advierte de una condición para la que debes prepararte. El blanco con texto negro es reglamentario, es decir, la regla es exigible. El verde te guía hacia destinos, el azul señala servicios como combustible, comida y alojamiento, y el naranja indica obras o mantenimiento. El marrón resalta lugares recreativos y culturales. Aprender estos patrones te permite leer una señal de un vistazo, incluso cuando el texto es pequeño o está tapado en parte por un camión. Ese instante cuenta cuando eliges un carril o reduces la velocidad por algo que aún no puedes ver.

entries.title: Señales reglamentarias
entries.text: Señales reglamentarias. Las señales reglamentarias te indican lo que debes o no debes hacer, y desobedecerlas es una infracción de tránsito. Ejemplos comunes son las señales de límite de velocidad, las de alto y ceda el paso, prohibido el paso, sentido único y no girar en rojo. La mayoría son blancas con marcas negras o rojas y se colocan donde la regla entra en vigor, no mucho antes. Una señal de límite de velocidad indica la velocidad máxima legal en buenas condiciones. Es un tope, no un objetivo que debas alcanzar, por lo que puedes circular más despacio cuando el clima, el tráfico o la superficie de la vía hacen que la velocidad publicada sea insegura. Las señales como no estacionar o no girar a la izquierda se aplican exactamente donde están colocadas y pueden incluir horarios o días específicos. Cuando una señal reglamentaria aparece junto a una preventiva, la reglamentaria rige la norma y la preventiva solo te avisa de lo que viene. Leer la señal completa, incluidas las flechas y el texto pequeño, evita confusiones en intersecciones donde coinciden varias reglas.

entries.title: Señales preventivas
entries.text: Señales preventivas. Las señales preventivas suelen ser rombos amarillos con símbolos negros y te alertan de un cambio en las condiciones de la vía más adelante. No crean una regla por sí mismas; te dicen que reduzcas la velocidad, observes y te prepares para ajustar. Ejemplos son curva adelante, intersección adelante, cruce de peatones, resbaladizo cuando llueve y cruce de animales. Algunas señales preventivas añaden una pequeña placa rectangular debajo, como una velocidad sugerida para una curva o la distancia hasta la condición. Un rombo amarillo con el símbolo de un semáforo advierte que hay una señal luminosa adelante y que puede ser difícil de ver. Un rombo con dos flechas opuestas muestra la dirección en la que se curva la vía. Como las señales preventivas describen peligros que aún no ves, la respuesta correcta es soltar el acelerador y observar la vía más adelante. Pasar a toda velocidad junto a una señal preventiva te deja sin tiempo para reaccionar si el peligro resulta ser tal como se describe.

entries.title: Señales informativas y de servicios
entries.text: Señales informativas y de servicios. Las señales informativas te dirigen a destinos, rutas y servicios, y son informativas más que reglamentarias. Las señales verdes con texto blanco muestran salidas, distancias y nombres de autopistas. Las azules señalan servicios como combustible, comida, alojamiento y hospitales. Las marrones indican parques, sitios históricos y zonas recreativas. En las interestatales, las señales informativas te dicen qué carril necesitas con antelación a la salida para que cambies de carril con calma. Los marcadores de milla te ayudan a describir tu ubicación si llamas pidiendo ayuda. Los indicadores de ruta identifican carreteras numeradas, incluidas las rutas federales y las rutas estatales de Florida. Las señales informativas son fáciles de leer si las buscas con antelación, pero nunca debes detenerte ni girar bruscamente para alcanzar una. Si te pasas una salida, continúa hasta la siguiente en lugar de retroceder o cruzar la mediana, lo cual es ilegal y peligroso.

entries.title: Señales de zonas de obras
entries.text: Señales de zonas de obras. Las señales naranjas y los dispositivos de canalización marcan zonas de construcción y mantenimiento, y a menudo incluyen límites de velocidad temporales. El naranja advierte de trabajadores, equipo y pavimento cambiante. Las multas por exceso de velocidad en una zona de obras pueden ser mayores de lo habitual, y el símbolo de un abanderado significa que una persona puede estar controlando el tráfico con una paleta. Las zonas de obras pueden cambiar de un día para otro, por lo que el carril que usaste ayer puede estar cerrado hoy. Reduce la velocidad en cuanto veas la primera señal naranja, aumenta el espacio delante de ti y sigue las indicaciones de los abanderados y las marcas del pavimento aunque difieran del patrón habitual. Los choques por alcance son frecuentes en las zonas de obras porque el tráfico se frena de forma inesperada. Observar los vehículos varios autos más adelante, y no solo el que tienes justo delante, te da más aviso cuando el tráfico se concentra.

entries.title: Leer señales con rapidez
entries.text: Leer señales con rapidez. Los buenos conductores leen las señales con antelación y las procesan sin quedarse mirando. Mantén los ojos en movimiento para captar una señal mientras aún es legible y después vuelve la mirada a la vía. Usar primero la forma y el color, y después el texto, te permite entender el mensaje en un instante. Las señales se colocan donde los conductores pueden verlas y reaccionar, así que si una señal te sorprende, quizá circulas demasiado rápido para las condiciones o no observas lo suficiente hacia adelante. Las grandes señales elevadas de las autopistas están diseñadas para leerse desde lejos, pero aun así debes elegir tu carril con antelación. Si el resplandor, la lluvia o la oscuridad reducen la visibilidad, reduce la velocidad y aumenta la distancia de seguimiento para poder leer las señales a tiempo. Unos faros limpios y un parabrisas despejado también facilitan ver las señales de noche.

entries.title: Semáforos y marcas viales
entries.text: Semáforos y marcas viales. Los semáforos y las marcas del pavimento te indican cuándo detenerte, cuándo avanzar y dónde está tu carril. Esta lección explica las señales fijas e intermitentes, las flechas de giro y el significado de las líneas blancas y amarillas para que interpretes la propia superficie de la vía.

entries.title: Señales luminosas fijas
entries.text: Señales luminosas fijas. Una luz roja fija significa detenerse por completo en la línea de detención, antes del paso de peatones o antes de la intersección cuando no hay línea. Ya detenido, generalmente puedes girar a la derecha salvo que una señal lo prohíba, y puedes girar a la izquierda desde una vía de un solo sentido hacia otra de un solo sentido, tras ceder el paso a peatones y tráfico. Una luz amarilla fija significa que la señal está a punto de ponerse roja. No significa acelerar. Si puedes detenerte con seguridad, hazlo; si ya estás dentro de la intersección o demasiado cerca para detenerte con seguridad, avanza con precaución y despeja la intersección. Una luz verde fija significa que puedes avanzar si el camino está libre. El verde no garantiza la prioridad de paso, así que aún debes ceder el paso a los peatones, a los vehículos que siguen en la intersección y al tráfico en sentido contrario cuando giras a la izquierda. Las flechas verdes dan movimiento protegido en la dirección indicada.

entries.title: Señales intermitentes y flechas
entries.text: Señales intermitentes y flechas. Una luz roja intermitente funciona como una señal de alto: detente por completo, cede el paso según sea necesario y avanza cuando sea seguro. Una luz amarilla intermitente significa reducir la velocidad y avanzar con precaución, atento al tráfico cruzado y a los peligros. Una flecha amarilla intermitente permite girar en esa dirección tras ceder el paso. Algunos semáforos están apagados por un fallo eléctrico o una avería. Trata un semáforo apagado como un alto de cuatro vías: detente, luego avanza en el orden en que llegaste y cede el paso al tráfico que ya está en la intersección. No supongas que el tráfico cruzado tiene luz roja cuando la señal no funciona. Algunas intersecciones usan una flecha verde seguida de una flecha amarilla intermitente para el mismo giro. La flecha verde protege el giro, mientras que la flecha amarilla intermitente significa que el giro está permitido pero el conductor debe ceder el paso al tráfico en sentido contrario.

entries.title: Marcas blancas del pavimento
entries.text: Marcas blancas del pavimento. Las líneas blancas separan el tráfico que se mueve en la misma dirección. Una línea blanca discontinua simple significa que puedes cambiar de carril cuando sea seguro, mientras que una línea blanca continua desaconseja los cambios de carril y una línea blanca continua doble significa que no debes cruzarla. Las líneas blancas también marcan el borde de la calzada y el límite derecho de tu carril. Las marcas blancas delimitan pasos de peatones, líneas de detención, flechas de giro y palabras como ONLY que indican que un carril está reservado para un movimiento específico. Una línea blanca continua que cruza tu carril antes de una intersección es la línea de detención donde debes parar ante una señal de alto o una luz roja. Las flechas pintadas en blanco muestran qué dirección debe seguir cada carril. Si un carril está marcado con una flecha de giro a la izquierda, debes girar a la izquierda desde él en lugar de seguir recto, así que elige tu carril con antelación a la intersección.

entries.title: Marcas amarillas del pavimento
entries.text: Marcas amarillas del pavimento. Las líneas amarillas separan el tráfico que se mueve en direcciones opuestas. Una línea amarilla discontinua significa que puedes cruzarla para adelantar cuando sea seguro y legal, mientras que una línea amarilla continua desaconseja el adelantamiento y cruzar para adelantar está generalmente prohibido. Una línea amarilla continua doble significa que ninguna dirección puede cruzarla para adelantar. Cuando un lado de una línea amarilla doble es continuo y el otro es discontinuo, el conductor del lado discontinuo puede adelantar si es seguro, mientras que el conductor del lado continuo no puede. Estas líneas muestran al tráfico en sentido contrario dónde puede esperar movimientos conflictivos. Una línea amarilla continua también marca el borde izquierdo de una autopista dividida o un carril central de giro. Un carril central compartido delimitado por líneas amarillas continua y discontinua se usa para girar a la izquierda en cualquier dirección, nunca para adelantar o circular con normalidad.

entries.title: Marcas especiales
entries.text: Marcas especiales. Las marcas del paso de peatones advierten a los conductores que esperen peatones, estén o no visibles en ese momento. Incluso un paso de peatones sin marcar en una intersección es un cruce legal, por lo que debes ceder el paso a los peatones que cruzan allí. Detente antes del paso para no bloquearlo. Las marcas de cruce de ferrocarril, las líneas blancas transversales y una X amarilla con las letras RR advierten de un cruce de ferrocarril adelante. Una X amarilla con la palabra ONLY puede marcar un carril reservado para un movimiento específico, y los símbolos de rombo en un carril pueden indicar un carril de uso especial o de vehículos de alta ocupación. Las islas pintadas en blanco y los patrones en cheurón muestran áreas sobre las que no debes circular. Las bandas rugosas, los marcadores elevados y las medianas pintadas guían el tráfico y separan movimientos opuestos, sobre todo donde los carriles se desplazan, como en plazas de peaje o enlaces.

entries.title: Girar a la derecha en rojo
entries.text: Girar a la derecha en rojo. En Florida, generalmente puedes girar a la derecha con una luz roja fija después de detenerte por completo, salvo que una señal indique no girar en rojo. Antes de girar, cede el paso a los peatones en el paso y al tráfico que se aproxima desde la izquierda, y luego completa el giro hacia el carril más cercano cuando esté libre. Como girar a la derecha en rojo es un movimiento permitido y no protegido, la responsabilidad recae en ti de asegurarte de que el camino sea seguro. Mira a la izquierda, luego otra vez a la izquierda y revisa de nuevo el paso de peatones, ya que un peatón o un ciclista puede estar oculto por los vehículos detenidos. Si hay una señal, una flecha roja o una señal roja fija con un cartel prohibitivo, debes esperar una luz verde o una flecha de giro. En caso de duda, esperar siempre es aceptable y nunca es una infracción.

entries.title: Prioridad de paso
entries.text: Prioridad de paso. La prioridad de paso no se toma, se cede. Esta lección explica quién pasa primero en intersecciones, altos de cuatro vías y pasos de peatones, y cómo ceder el paso a vehículos de emergencia y peatones de forma segura.

entries.title: Cómo funcionan las intersecciones
entries.text: Cómo funcionan las intersecciones. Las reglas de prioridad de paso mantienen el tráfico en un orden predecible cuando las trayectorias se cruzan, y existen para evitar la confusión, no para premiar la velocidad. El principio básico es que cedes el paso al tráfico que ya está en la intersección y al que tiene la prioridad legal, y solo avanzas cuando es seguro. Los semáforos, las señales y las marcas del pavimento normalmente indican quién pasa primero. Donde ninguno de ellos controla la intersección, se aplican reglas estándar: cede el paso al vehículo de tu derecha y cede el paso al tráfico de la vía más grande o principal cuando entras desde una más pequeña. El conductor que tiene la prioridad de paso aún debe estar listo para cederla y evitar un choque. La ley puede decir que un conductor tenía prioridad, pero eso no protege a nadie de las lesiones, así que el conductor defensivo vigila a quienes podrían no ceder.

entries.title: Altos de cuatro vías
entries.text: Altos de cuatro vías. En un alto de cuatro vías, el primer vehículo que se detiene es el primero que avanza. Si dos vehículos llegan casi al mismo tiempo, el conductor de la izquierda cede el paso al de la derecha. Si varios vehículos llegan juntos, cada uno avanza por turno, normalmente en orden de las agujas del reloj. La clave es detenerse por completo, no solo reducir. Una vez detenido, observa a los demás conductores para asegurarte de que ellos también piensan detenerse, porque a veces las personas calculan mal quién llegó primero. Haz contacto visual o usa un gesto claro cuando tengas dudas. No le indiques a otro conductor que pase si eso crea confusión con el resto del tráfico. En un alto de cuatro vías concurrido, el enfoque más seguro es tomar tu turno de forma predecible y avanzar solo cuando el cruce de la intersección esté realmente libre.

entries.title: Intersecciones sin control
entries.text: Intersecciones sin control. Una intersección sin control no tiene señales ni semáforos que indiquen quién pasa primero. Cuando dos vehículos llegan casi al mismo tiempo, el conductor de la izquierda debe ceder el paso al vehículo de la derecha. Cuando entras a una vía principal desde una lateral o una entrada, cedes el paso al tráfico que ya está en la vía principal. Las intersecciones sin control suelen aparecer en zonas residenciales donde la visibilidad está limitada por autos estacionados, setos o esquinas. Acércate a una velocidad suficientemente baja para poder detenerte si aparece un vehículo, un peatón o un ciclista, y mantén el pie sobre el freno para reaccionar al instante. Un vehículo que gira a la izquierda también debe ceder el paso al tráfico en sentido contrario que sigue recto o gira a la derecha. Haber llegado primero no le da permiso al conductor que gira a la izquierda para cruzar el tráfico que se aproxima antes de que sea seguro.

entries.title: Peatones y pasos de peatones
entries.text: Peatones y pasos de peatones. Los peatones generalmente tienen la prioridad de paso en los pasos de peatones y en las intersecciones, esté o no pintado el paso. Debes ceder y con frecuencia detenerte ante un peatón que está en tu carril o cruza hacia él, y no debes rebasar a un vehículo que se ha detenido por un peatón. Los peatones ciegos pueden usar un bastón blanco o un perro guía, y siempre tienen la prioridad de paso en un paso de peatones e incluso fuera de uno en ciertas situaciones. Dales bastante espacio y tiempo, y nunca toques el claxon para apurar a un peatón, ya que eso puede hacer que alguien tropiece. Un peatón que cruza fuera del paso, es decir, fuera de un cruce donde hay señales, comete una infracción, pero los conductores aún deben evitar atropellar a cualquiera. Ceder con prontitud evita una emergencia y mantiene a todos más seguros, sin importar quién tenga técnicamente la prioridad.

entries.title: Vehículos de emergencia y especiales
